title: Fearless, changeless
hook: the Jaap keeps returning to fearlessness, a quality at the heart of the Khalsa ideal

segments.voice: Yesterday, ek achhari, and your line, ajai, alai, abhai, abai. Did you say them once when the day pushed back? Today, the third of those four words, the one Jaap keeps coming back to. Day three hundred fifty-two.

Fear has a body. A tight chest before the phone call. Cold hands before the exam results open. A stomach that drops when the boss says, got a minute? Plenty of people carry a few fears around like stones in a pocket: money, health, being left, being found out. We get so used to the weight that we forget it's there, until something makes us reach in and touch one. Jaap Sahib, recited every morning, keeps saying one word against that weight. Today: fearless, changeless.
screen: `FEAR HAS A BODY.` → `STONES IN A POCKET.` → `A WORD SAID AGAINST THE WEIGHT.`

segments.voice: The word is abhai. Bhai is fear; a is without. Fearless. Count how often it comes back in Jaap. It's in the one-letter meter, ajai, alai, abhai, abai. It returns again and again in other stanzas, alongside its partners: unconquerable, unchanging, unborn. Of all the qualities Jaap praises, fearlessness is one it simply won't let go of. Sikhs met the idea long before Jaap. The Mool Mantar, at the very start of the Guru Granth Sahib, calls the One nirbhau, without fear, and nirvair, without hatred, side by side. Guru Nanak's opening and the Tenth Guru's praise agree. Then comes the turn that matters for daily life. Sikhs don't praise fearlessness only as something God has. They hope to grow toward it. The ninth Guru, Guru Tegh Bahadur, the Tenth Guru's father, wrote that the wise person is the one who frightens no one, and fears no one. Both halves. Not a bully, and not a coward. And Sikhs remember him living it: tradition tells of him going to Delhi and to his execution rather than abandon the freedom of others to practice their faith. Fearlessness sits at the heart of the Khalsa ideal his son founded: a people meant to stand up without fear and without hate, and never to put fear into the innocent. That's the logic of the carry, as Sikh teachers often put it: people grow a little like what they praise every morning. Saying abhai doesn't make fear vanish. The hope is that fear stops being the one deciding.
screen: `ABHAI: WITHOUT FEAR.` · `NIRBHAU, NIRVAIR: THE MOOL MANTAR.` · `FRIGHTEN NO ONE, FEAR NO ONE.` · `GROWING LIKE WHAT YOU PRAISE.` · then, large: `FEARLESS LIKE HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one fear and breathe. Reach into the pocket and pick up one stone. Name it, silently and plainly: I'm afraid of this. Notice where it sits in your body: chest, stomach, shoulders, jaw. Breathe into that place, slowly, without trying to make the fear leave. Just let it be held. Then, if you like, say abhai on the out-breath, a few times. Not to argue with the fear. Just to remind it who else is here. The bell holds the time.
Abhai. Without fear: the quality Jaap keeps returning to, echoing nirbhau in the Mool Mantar.
Your line: fearless like him. Today, do one small thing you've been putting off out of fear, and do it without frightening anyone else. Day three hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: Sikhs say nirbhau, without fear, every day in the Mool Mantar and abhai many times in Jaap Sahib, and fearlessness without hatred is central to the Khalsa ideal.

pairs: without fear, in the Mool Mantar
fear no one, frighten no one

myth: fearlessness appears only once in Jaap
abhai keeps coming back, beside unconquerable, unchanging and unborn.
the Mool Mantar pairs fearless with without hatred
Guru Tegh Bahadur praised those who make others afraid
he called wise the one who frightens no one and fears no one.

fork.setup: Guru Tegh Bahadur describes the wise person in two halves. which pair is it?
options: fears no one, and frightens no one.
fears nothing, and cares about nothing.
fork.reveal: not a bully and not a coward: the wise one neither gives fear nor takes it (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1427).

original.note: Gurmukhi: abhai, without fear, from bhai, fear; compare nirbhau in the Mool Mantar.

trapdoor: what you thought: fearless is a quality only God has.
what it means: Sikhs praise the One as fearless and hope to grow toward it, frightening no one and fearing no one.
what a scholar hears: abhai in Jaap parallels nirbhau in the Mool Mantar; Guru Tegh Bahadur's salok at Ang 1427 sets out the human ideal.

sources.ref: Jaap Sahib: abhai (ek achhari and other stanzas)
Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1 (Mool Mantar): nirbhau, nirvair

notes: The outline calls fearlessness 'the gift the Khalsa asks for'; the voice says instead that fearlessness 'sits at the heart of the Khalsa ideal', since no specific Ardas line asking for fearlessness was confirmed. Keeper may wish to adjust.
Guru Tegh Bahadur, Ang 1427 ('bhai kaahu ko det neh, neh bhai maanat aan...') paraphrased: confirm Ang.
Hook changed from 'the gift the Khalsa asks for' to 'a quality at the heart of the Khalsa ideal' to match the voice, pending a confirmed source.

Guru Tegh Bahadur's execution in Delhi (1675), framed as defending others' freedom to practice their faith: now attributed to Sikh tradition ('Sikhs remember', 'tradition tells') since historians frame the motives differently; confirm the Keeper's preferred wording.
Editor review (2026-10-01): removed 'Most of us' and the 'Now imagine' hook turn; 'you become like what you praise' now attributed to Sikh teachers rather than stated by the narrator.
